en: DeepSeek shrank a model's memory of past words to 4 percent. And it scored better.
Not worse: better, in their own tests at least. How? With a vacuum pump, a pair of glasses and a luggage tag. From Prof. Yufei Ding's CSE 291P, lectures 3 and 4.
Quick callback. At the attention party, every token, a word or a piece of one, carries a question card, its query; a name tag, its key; and a parcel, its value.
The KV cache is the cloakroom: a wall of tags and parcels for every earlier guest. Last time, grouped-query attention let groups of heads, the parallel copies of attention, share one rack.
This time the clerk packs. This is multi-head latent attention, from DeepSeek's V2 paper. Instead of making heads share, it compresses.
The clerk puts a guest's tag and parcel into one clear bag, and pumps the air out. One flat pouch.
In the model, the pouch is a latent vector: a short hidden summary, learned in training. A learned matrix, W-down, squeezes the token into it. Multiplying by a learned matrix is called a projection.
One pouch per token per layer, holding both the key and the value. Every head can get its own key and value back out of it.
How flat? In DeepSeek-V2 the pouch holds 512 numbers, as long as four keys of 128, against 32,768 for the keys and values of all 128 heads.
Where the picture stops: a vacuum bag gives back exactly what went in. This squeeze is learned, and the model trains with it from the start.
Here is the first catch. To read a pouch, the clerk would unpack it: two more learned matrices, W-UK and W-UV, rebuild the name tag and the parcel.
And that for every earlier guest, at every new step: the very work the cache was meant to save.
The way out is an optician. How well the new question matches an old name tag is a score: the key times the query. And the key is W-UK times the pouch.
Matrix products can be regrouped: the brackets move, the order stays. Her slide calls it the associative property. So W-UK can be multiplied into the query side first.
The optician grinds the unpacking into the guest's glasses. And the parcel's unpacking, W-UV, folds into the output matrix, the last multiplication, which mixes the heads' results.
The glasses are the same for every pouch on the table.
The loop runs over every earlier token. So the glasses are made once per new token and head, not once per pouch.
And the guest reads the whole row of sealed pouches through them. Nothing is unpacked.
A model has to know word order. RoPE, rotary position embedding, is the usual way to mark it: it turns each query and key by an angle set by its position, like a clock hand.

Now every key is turned by its own angle, after it comes out of the pouch. In her derivation, that turn lands between the question and W-UK, and it is different for every earlier token. Factors may regroup, but never swap places. So no single pair of glasses fits them all. Every key would have to be rebuilt again.
The fix: keep position out of the pouch. The keys that come out of it are never turned, so the glasses still fit.

Instead, each token gets a small separate luggage tag, 64 numbers, made from the token itself, turned by its position, and cached beside the pouch. Each head reads it with a small turned piece of its question.
Her slide: separate what from where. And one tag per token, shared by every head. Her slide's reason: where a word sits is the same for every head.
Now the size. Per token per layer: the 512-number pouch plus the 64-number tag. 576 numbers, as long as four and a half keys.

A group keeps one key and one value, 128 numbers each: 256. And 576 over 256 is two and a quarter. So this is the cache of grouped-query attention with just two and a quarter groups, whatever the number of heads.
Her worksheet tries it on Llama 3's three shapes, as if every head kept its own keys and values: 32 layers and 32 heads, 80 and 64, 126 and 128.

For the smallest, at two bytes a number: 36 kilobytes per token in her table, instead of 512. Fourteen times smaller. Then 28 times, and more than 56. Even against Llama 3's real eight-group cache, about 3.6 times smaller: eight groups against two and a quarter.
And the quality? In DeepSeek's own tests, at two model sizes, the compressed version kept 4 to 14 percent of the cache, and scored higher on seven of eight benchmark scores.
Why would a squeeze help? She offers guesses, and calls them guesses.
Dropout: switch off random parts of a network while it trains, and it often does better. A squeeze can be a trim that keeps the hedge healthy.
Plain attention may pack the same shirt many times over. And keeping position apart may stop it muddling the content.
These are the authors' own runs, and their next report calls the quality comparable to plain attention. Their next model, V3, kept the design.
One last catch. Inside attention, the glasses read every pouch whole: 512 numbers wide, where one head would read 128. Several times more arithmetic for every remembered token.

Generating word by word, memory is the bottleneck: a good trade. But reading a whole prompt, the folded form takes about three times the arithmetic. So engines like vLLM switch: unpack for the prompt, fold for generating. Either way, the cache itself stays packed.
So: pack each token into one learned pouch, and read it through glasses instead of unpacking it. Keep position on its own small tag: a cache the size of just two and a quarter groups.
Next time: the residual highway.
